body.heading: Order is what makes a crystal
paragraphs: A crystal is a solid whose atoms or molecules are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern, like bricks in a wall that extends in every direction. That internal order is why crystals so often have flat faces and sharp, geometric shapes: the outside of the crystal is the inside pattern, written large.

Crystals grow from liquids or solutions. Dissolve as much of a substance as hot water will hold, then let the water cool or evaporate, and the liquid becomes over-full — supersaturated. The dissolved particles must come out, and when they settle they do not land randomly: each one locks into the pattern, guided by the ones already in place.

body.heading: Layer by layer
paragraphs: Growth starts with nucleation, the formation of a tiny first cluster — sometimes on a speck of dust or a thread deliberately hung in the solution. From that seed, particles arriving from the liquid attach to the growing faces, extending the pattern layer by layer. Rock-candy makers exploit exactly this: a sugary syrup, a stick, and patience.

Speed decides quality. Grow slowly and each particle has time to find its proper place, producing large, clear, well-formed crystals. Rush it — chill the solution suddenly — and countless tiny crystals form at once, giving a cloudy, grainy mass instead. Fudge-makers stir and cool quickly on purpose, precisely to keep the sugar crystals too small to feel on the tongue.

body.heading: Crystals that run the world
paragraphs: Nature grows crystals underground over millions of years: quartz veins, gemstones, and cave crystals longer than the room they are read about in. Ice is a crystal too — every snowflake is water grown into a six-sided pattern in the air.

Industry grows them on demand. The silicon at the heart of every computer chip begins as a single crystal pulled slowly from molten silicon into a cylinder longer than a person is tall, then sliced into wafers thinner than a credit card. One flawless crystal, grown layer by layer, becomes the foundation of all modern electronics.
